etymology: Radical from Latin radix, “root”—here naming the construal that goes to a sharper root than the classical Reformed doctrine. The label Radical Two Kingdoms (commonly R2K) was coined by critics within the Reformed world to distinguish the late-20th-century Westminster Seminary California revival—principally D. G. Hart, David VanDrunen, and Michael Horton—from the older confessional Lutheran and Reformed two-kingdoms doctrine of Luther, Calvin, and the Reformed orthodox.
biblical_def: Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K) is a particular late-twentieth-century construal of the Reformed two-kingdoms doctrine, associated principally with Westminster Seminary California (D. G. Hart, David VanDrunen, Michael Horton), which goes substantively further than the older confessional 2K in four directions and is therefore distinguished from it under its own name. First, R2K sharpens the Creator-Redeemer distinction in spheres: Christ’s mediatorial (redemptive) kingship is exercised over the church, while His kingship over the civil order is treated as His kingship as Creator, not as Mediator—so that the civil sphere is what VanDrunen calls the common kingdom, governed by natural law and not by the redemptive purposes of Christ’s mediatorial reign. Second, R2K restricts the civil kingdom to natural law as its governing standard, holding that Scripture’s civil and judicial content was tied to Israel’s peculiar theocratic situation and is not to be normatively reapplied to modern magistrates, who are to govern by reason and natural law accessible to all men. Third, R2K applies a sharpened ‘spirituality of the church’ doctrine: the institutional church’s public-square voice is restricted to gospel proclamation and the cure of souls, with the church as church declining to address civil questions (abortion, marriage, the magistrate’s duty), though individual Christians are free to engage politically in their personal vocations. Fourth, R2K’s eschatology holds that the present civil order is being preserved, not redeemed, and that cultural transformation is not part of the church’s mission; the redeemed creation awaits the consummation, and the present age’s cultural products will not carry over into the new earth. Each of these four moves goes further than the classical Lutheran and Reformed 2K position represented by Calvin’s Institutes IV.20, the Belgic Confession 36, the Westminster Confession 23, and the Reformed orthodox political theology of the 17th c.—and it is precisely the gap between the older confessional 2K and these four R2K modifications that makes the qualifier radical a doctrinal description rather than a slur.
webster_summary: (Composite.) A specific late-20th-c. construal of two-kingdoms theology, associated with Westminster Seminary California, which limits the civil sphere to natural law, restricts the church’s institutional voice on civil questions, and sharpens the Creator/Redeemer distinction between Christ’s kingship over church and world—going further than the classical confessional 2K of Luther, Calvin, the Belgic, and Westminster.
webster_full: RADICAL TWO KINGDOMS (R2K), n. (Reformed political-theological position, late 20th c.) A specific construal of two-kingdoms doctrine articulated principally at Westminster Seminary California (D. G. Hart, David VanDrunen, Michael Horton), distinguished from the older confessional Lutheran and Reformed 2K by four substantive moves: (1) a sharpened Creator/Redeemer distinction such that Christ’s mediatorial kingship is exercised over the church and His kingship over the civil order is exercised as Creator; (2) the restriction of the civil kingdom to natural-law standards, treating Scripture’s civil/judicial content as tied to Israel’s peculiar theocratic situation and not normative for modern magistrates; (3) a sharpened ‘spirituality of the church’ restricting the institutional church’s voice on civil questions; (4) an eschatology in which the present civil order is preserved but not redeemed, and cultural transformation is not part of the church’s mission. The label radical, originating in critical Reformed discussion, marks the gap between this construal and the classical confessional 2K of Calvin, the Belgic Confession 36 (pre-1905 revision), and the Westminster Confession 23 (pre-1788 American revision).

corruption_summary: R2K corrupts the older confessional two-kingdoms doctrine by sharply dividing Christ’s kingship over church and world along Creator/Redeemer lines, by restricting the civil sphere to natural law that has empirically failed to persuade late-modern magistrates on the very questions where Scripture commands prophetic witness, by silencing the institutional church on those questions in principle, and by an eschatology that surrenders cultural ground in advance—each move going further than Calvin, Belgic 36, and WCF 23 in their original confessional form.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-confessional objection to R2K is that it is not, despite its self-presentation, simply the classical Reformed two-kingdoms doctrine. Calvin’s Institutes IV.20 has the civil magistrate as a positive minister of God charged with the care of true religion, not merely a natural-law preserver of public order. The Belgic Confession of 1561, article 36, originally charged the magistrate to remove and prevent all idolatry and false worship, that the kingdom of antichrist may be thus destroyed and the kingdom of Christ promoted—language so substantial that the Dutch Reformed churches did not omit it until 1905, and which the original Westminster Confession 23 likewise preserves in its pre-1788 form. R2K cannot recover this confessional content; it must instead treat its own narrowing—civil sphere as natural-law-only, magistrate as religiously neutral preserver—as a development beyond the original Reformed confessions, even where it claims to be merely recovering them. The qualifier radical is therefore not pejorative shorthand; it is the precise term for a position that has cut a more recent root than the classical confessional one, and the MOOP Dictionary stands with the older confessional 2K against the modern narrowing.

The pastoral and exegetical objections sharpen the historical one. Pastorally, R2K’s working political theology has, in late modernity, produced something approaching the functional silence that both R2K and its critics formally reject: when the magistrate authorizes the killing of children in the womb, redefines marriage, and prosecutes confessing believers under sexual-orientation and gender-identity codes, the natural-law standard R2K calls upon has not in fact persuaded post-Christian magistrates, and the institutional church it has trained to silence on civil questions has been correspondingly absent at the very hours its prophetic voice was most needed. A doctrine whose consistent application produces silence where Scripture commands witness—be wise now therefore, O ye kings... kiss the Son, lest he be angry—needs reworking. Exegetically, the sharp Creator-Redeemer compartmentalization on which R2K relies is hard to maintain against Eph 1:22 (the Father hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church), 1 Cor 15:25 (Christ must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet—a present mediatorial reign over all things), Heb 1:2-3 (the Son who upholds all things by the word of His power is the same Son appointed heir of all things), and Matt 28:18 (all power is given unto me in heaven and in earth—the Great Commission begins from Christ’s universal mediatorial authority). The classical Reformed reading holds the two kingdoms distinct without bifurcating Christ’s kingship into separate Creator and Mediator offices in spheres; the magistrate is a minister of God under the Christ who reigns now over all things; the church speaks prophetically to civil order under the same Lord—and the result is neither the theocratic conflation R2K rightly rejects nor the silenced church R2K formally rejects but functionally produces.
roots_summary: Late-20th-c. Westminster Seminary California revival (Hart, VanDrunen, Horton) of two-kingdoms doctrine, distinguished from the older confessional Lutheran/Reformed 2K (Luther’s Zwei-Reiche-Lehre, Calvin’s Institutes IV.20, Belgic 36, WCF 23) by four substantive narrowings.

etymology: Reformed-confessional doctrine that God rules the world through two distinct kingdoms: a spiritual kingdom (the church, governed by Word and Spirit) and a civil kingdom (the magistrate, governed under God by law and the sword). Articulated by Luther (the Zwei-Reiche-Lehre), developed and integrated into Reformed political theology by Calvin (Institutes IV.20), confessed by the Reformed and Lutheran churches in the 16th–17th centuries (Belgic 36, WCF 23, Augsburg 16), and substantively narrowed in the late twentieth century by the Westminster Seminary California school into the position now distinguished under its own name as Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K).
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that God rules the world through two distinct but not unrelated kingdoms under the one universal mediatorial Lordship of Jesus Christ. The spiritual kingdom is the church, governed by Christ through Word and Spirit, gathered around Word and sacrament, advancing by gospel proclamation. The civil kingdom (or common kingdom) is the secular order of magistrate, family, vocation, and culture, governed under God by His ordinance of civil authority (Rom 13:1-4) and by His revealed and natural law together. Christ is Lord of both kingdoms; the two are distinct in office, sphere, and means, but not bifurcated into separate Creator and Redeemer kingships in spheres—He reigns now, mediatorially, over all things, for the church (Eph 1:22; 1 Cor 15:25). The MOOP Dictionary stands with the classical confessional 2K of Luther, Calvin, the Belgic Confession 36 (in its original form), and the Westminster Confession 23 (in its original form)—which distinguishes the spheres without evacuating the magistrate’s duty toward true religion and without silencing the church’s prophetic voice on civil questions. The doctrine is distinguished in this dictionary from the late-20th-century Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K) construal of Westminster Seminary California (D. G. Hart, David VanDrunen, Michael Horton), which goes substantively further—restricting the civil sphere to natural law only, silencing the institutional church on civil questions in principle, and bifurcating Christ’s kingship over church and world along Creator/Redeemer lines. R2K is treated under its own entry, where its four substantive narrowings and the confessional Reformed objections to them are set out at length.
webster_summary: Reformed doctrine of two distinct kingdoms (spiritual / civil) under the one mediatorial Lordship of Christ; distinguished here from the late-20th-c. Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K) narrowing, which receives its own entry.
webster_full: TWO KINGDOMS THEOLOGY, n. (Reformed political-theological doctrine, 16th c. onward) The position that God rules the world through two distinct kingdoms—the spiritual kingdom of the church, governed by Word and Spirit, and the civil kingdom of the magistrate, governed under God by His ordinance of civil authority and by His law—both under the one mediatorial Lordship of Jesus Christ, who reigns now over all things for the church. Articulated by Luther (the Zwei-Reiche-Lehre), developed by Calvin in Institutes IV.20, and confessed by the Reformed and Lutheran churches in the 16th–17th centuries (Belgic 36, WCF 23, Augsburg 16), the doctrine in its classical confessional form preserves the distinction of the spheres without evacuating the magistrate’s duty toward true religion or silencing the church’s prophetic voice on civil questions. In late-20th-c. America the doctrine was substantively narrowed by the Westminster Seminary California school (D. G. Hart, David VanDrunen, Michael Horton) into the position now distinguished under the label Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K), which is treated under its own entry.

corruption_summary: Two-kingdoms language is corrupted, on one side, by collapsing the spheres into the medieval-Constantinian conflation the Reformers labored to correct; and on the other—and far more common today—by the late-20th-c. Westminster California narrowing distinguished here as Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K), which restricts the civil sphere to natural law only, silences the institutional church on civil questions in principle, and bifurcates Christ’s mediatorial kingship along Creator/Redeemer lines.
corruption_paragraphs: The older corruption is the medieval-Constantinian conflation in which the magistrate is treated as the executive arm of the church, with no distinction of office or sphere. The Reformers labored to correct this, articulating the two-kingdoms doctrine partly to protect both the freedom of the church and the proper authority of the civil magistrate from each other’s overreach. The classical confessional 2K position therefore neither identifies the kingdoms with each other nor surrenders the magistrate’s positive duty toward true religion—Calvin’s Institutes IV.20, the original Belgic 36, and the original WCF 23 stand as the confessional benchmark.

The more pressing modern corruption—and the one most likely to be mistaken for two-kingdoms doctrine simpliciter—is the late-20th-c. Westminster Seminary California narrowing for which Reformed critics have coined the label Radical Two Kingdoms (R2K). R2K goes substantively further than the older confessional 2K in four directions: (1) it bifurcates Christ’s kingship over church and world along Creator/Redeemer lines; (2) it restricts the civil sphere to natural-law standards, treating Scripture’s civil/judicial content as tied to Israel’s peculiar theocratic situation and not normative for modern magistrates; (3) it sharpens the ‘spirituality of the church’ doctrine into a near-total restriction on the institutional church’s voice on civil questions; and (4) it teaches an eschatology in which the present civil order is preserved but not redeemed, with cultural transformation excluded from the church’s mission. The MOOP Dictionary distinguishes this R2K construal from the classical confessional 2K of Luther, Calvin, and the original Reformed confessions, treats R2K at its own entry where the four moves and the confessional Reformed objections to them are set out at length, and stands with the older 2K position against the modern narrowing. Be wise now therefore, O ye kings... kiss the Son, lest he be angry—the magistrate’s duty toward Christ remains, and the church’s prophetic voice on civil order is not to be silenced in principle.
